newsitem.title: FRANCE: Projected Socialist win to limit markets fall.
newsitem.headline: Projected Socialist win to limit markets fall.

text.p: A projected clear majority for the Socialist Party in Sunday's runoff parliamentary election vote was expected to mitigate falls on French financial markets, analysts and traders said.

Investors had feared a failure by the Socialists to attain an absolute majority of 289 seats in the lower house National Assembly would force them into a power-sharing deal with the Communists, who are outright opponents of the euro single currency and of social security reforms.

"It looks like the Socialists have an absolute majority so the market reaction may be rather soft," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance, said. "I would still say slightly negative but maybe not all that much."
The franc eased slightly against the mark but the fall was softened by the prospect of a Communist-free administration.
Projections from the BVA, SOFRES and CSA polliing institutes early on Sunday evening all showed the Socialists winning an outright majority in the National Assembly.
"I'm not expecting the franc to weaken that much. I think people had a target of 3.40 per mark if the Socialists did not have an absolute majority," Brossard said.
The franc was trading at 3.3822 per mark at 1840 GMT compared with 3.3816 late on Friday.

For Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris: "What is interesting is that the Socialists could have a majority alone, which is not so bad for markets. They would be less prone to be influenced by the Communists on both economic and European policies."
Of French markets the stockmarket fell most heavily after last Sunday's vote, losing six percent on the week. Share prices are expected to fall further, traders and analysts said.
Equities strategist Gary Dugan at J.P. Morgan said he expected the Paris bourse's CAC-40 index to fall next week but not more than three percent.
"This is better than the worst outcome, which would have been a heavy reliance on the Communists for an absolute majority," Dugan said.
Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, said: "It seems the Socialists are going to be able to form a government without the Communists. This is relatively good news."
The CAC-40, which finished down 6.48 percent last week at 2,583.94 points, could fall to 2,500. "I would be surprised to see it go much lower," she said.
But even though electoral uncertainty was over, French shares would continue to be penalised with a risk premium from uncertainty over the new government's programmes.

"We will be waiting on the lips of the politicians. There will be considerable volatility as announcements come through on policy decisions," Elisabetta Castelli, head of international equities CDC Bourse, said.
"We don't know whether France Telecom and Thomson-CSF will be privatised," Castelli said.

J.P. Morgan's Dugan said a decision on France Telecom's partial privatisation -- scheduled by the outgoing government to begin in the coming week -- would be the key "to judge how left-wing this government will be".
Carmaker Renault, whose restructuring plans may be put in doubt, is also likely to weaken further, he said.
